voce: Microsoft released a 2.3 billion-parameter model that runs on-device. It can handle a 32 K token context, enough for multi-page documents.

Aion-1.0-Instruct-2.3B is Microsoft’s small language model for the Windows ecosystem. The model runs in PyTorch, ONNX and GGUF formats and is released under the MIT license on Hugging Face. It supports English, German, Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, French, Chinese and Japanese, and is built for on-device text generation tasks like summarization, rewriting and chat.

According to the model card, Aion is the foundational Small Language Model for Windows, optimized for responsive, private AI without constant cloud calls. Positional encoding combines RoPE with YaRN scaling, enabling the long 32 K context. Microsoft released the unquantized version first, promising later quantized releases.

The model card lists several benchmark scores. On the MMLU knowledge test the model scored 55.15 percent, while on the multilingual MMMLU it reached 45.51 percent. In math, GSM8K gave 74.91 percent and GSMPlus 49.56 percent. Instruction following measured by IFEval was 83.90 percent, and translation quality (chrF++) was 43.18 percent. These numbers reflect a small model’s performance compared with larger systems.

Because it is only 2.3 B parameters, Aion loads quickly and fits on modest hardware, a RTX 4060 can hold it fully in GPU memory. Token throughput ranges from 135 tokens per second on an RTX 3060 up to 436 tokens per second on an RTX 5090. The model excels at short-form generation and on-device privacy. However, the card warns that small models often miss fine details, struggle with multi-step reasoning and can generate inaccurate statements. Safety alignment is present but not as robust as larger models.

Aion-1.0-Instruct-2.3B is aimed at people who run AI at home and want a free, open model that works offline. Its long context makes it useful for document summarization, email thread analysis and other multi-page tasks. If you need a model that respects privacy and runs on a mid-range GPU, this is a solid choice. Keep in mind its reasoning limits and verify outputs for critical applications.

What do you need to run it at home? At 4-bit it takes about 4 gigabytes of memory. The smallest home machine that holds it fully is an RTX 40 60. On an RTX 30 60 12 GB with 32 gigabytes of RAM it writes about 135 tokens per second. On an RTX 40 90 with 64 gigabytes of RAM it writes about 303 tokens per second.
There is no free API for it yet. The weights are open: you can download them from Hugging Face under the MIT license. Arena has not ranked it yet: we add the score as soon as the votes arrive.
